titleStmt.title: From Stranger to Parent: Duties of Care in Intentional Pregnancies

DAVID WASSERMAN *
From Stranger to Parent:
Duties of Care in Intentional
Pregnancies
I. INTRODUCTION
Two years before Roe v. Wade was decided, Judith Jarvis Thomson's land-
mark "Defense of Abortion" 1 attempted to shift the debate from the moral
status of the fetus to the pregnant person's right to control her own body:
she may enforce that right by withdrawing life-support from any being she
has not agreed to sustain, however high its moral status or strong its inter-
est in survival. 2 Thomson made this argument with what has become a
famous, or infamous, analogy:
You wake up in the morning and find yourself back to back in bed with
an unconscious violinist. A famous unconscious violinist. He has been
found to have a fatal kidney ailment, and the Society of Music Lovers
has canvassed all the available medical records and found that you
alone have the right blood type to help. They have therefore kidnapped
you, and last night the violinist's circulatory system was plugged into
yours, so that your kidneys can be used to extract poisons from his
blood as well as your own. . . "To unplug you would be to kill him [you
are told]. But never mind, it's only for nine months. By then he will

1. Judith Jarvis Thomson, "A Defense of Abortion," Philosophy & Public Affairs 1, no.
1 (1971): 47-66.
2. While I will adopt the more inclusive "pregnant person," I will use female pronouns for
clarity; a compromise that will satisfy no one. I will also adopt the term "intending mother" to
refer to any pregnant person who decides to parent the child-to-be.

Thomson argued that the pregnant person, like the person attached to the
violinist, has the right to withdraw life-support.
Over the years, Thomson's argument (as I will refer to it) has generated
a considerable literature, criticizing, defending, or qualifying her analogy.
My focus will be on a distinct objection: that it has implications for the
permissibility of prenatal injury so untenable that they must indicate a
fatal flaw. I will argue that these implications are not as untenable as they
may seem. Rather, much of the resistance they provoke arises from the
assumption that if the pregnant person chooses to continue the preg-
nancy, she cannot remain a stranger to the fetus, if she ever was one. By
choosing to carry the fetus to term or to the point where abortion is no
longer permissible, 4 she accepts duties of care that would rarely, if ever,
permit her to cause or allow significant prenatal injury, even injury that
would leave the child-to-be with a life well worth living. However, it
proves surprisingly difficult to explain how the decision to continue a
pregnancy, which abortion defenders regard as revocable far into gesta-
tion, can impose such duties.
The prenatal-injury objection was first raised (to the best of my knowl-
edge) by Jeff McMahan:
Since [the woman] would not owe it to the fetus to carry it to term and
would be justified in killing it in order to avoid the burden of carriage,
the fetus would, if the woman could not protect her interests without
either killing or injuring it, have to accept injury as the price of contin-
ued carriage. 5
3. Thomson, "Defense of Abortion," 48-49.
4. I will drop the second disjunct in what follows. I do so to keep the formulation simple,
not because I'm committed to the view that all late term abortions are permissible. For those
who hold that Thomson's argument only justifies abortion up to some point in pregnancy,
later abortions will compound, rather than preempt the wrong. Of course, for those who find
abortion generally impermissible, it will almost always compound the wrong.
5. Jeff McMahan, "Paradoxes of Abortion and Prenatal Injury," Ethics 116, no. 4 (2006):
625-55.

He concludes "[t]hat the Thomson argument has these implications casts
doubt on its plausibility." 6 Recently, Jessica Flanigan has defended the
implication McMahan finds untenable; she argues that a pregnant person
is praiseworthy for carrying the fetus to term and has no duty of prenatal
care beyond leaving the child-to-be with a life worth living. 7
I will begin with a highly qualified defense of Flanigan's claims about
the permissive implications of Thomson's argument. Although the preg-
nant person has less latitude than Flanigan claims, so long as she remains
a stranger to the fetus, she has no greater duty of care to it than she would
to any similarly dependent stranger. 8
I will then address two challenges to the claim that Thomson's argu-
ment has these implications. The first denies that abortion can serve as a
moral baseline for fetal care; it rejects the claim that the right to abort def-
ended by Thomson permits, a fortiori, any prenatal care that leaves the
fetus better off than abortion. The second challenge denies that a pregnant
person who decides to continue gestation can remain a stranger to the
fetus, rather than becoming a prospective parent or a proxy for one. In
addressing this challenge, I will offer a hypothetical case to illustrate how
a pregnant person could voluntarily carry a fetus to term without assum-
ing the role or acquiring the duties of an intending mother or proxy.
I then examine whether a pregnant person's decision to parent could
impose a more demanding duty of care if she remains free to abort. Her
freedom to do so may seem puzzling, since abortion would be worse for
the child-to-be than all but the most severe breaches of such a duty. 9 I
assess three grounds for denying that an intending mother remains free to
abort if she breaches her duty of care: because of the commitment she
has made; because of the injury she has caused or allowed; or because

7. Jessica Flanigan, "The Ethics of Prenatal Injury," Journal of Moral Philosophy 18, no.
1 (2021): 26-48.
8. A reviewer has suggested that Thomson's argument for the permissibility of abortion
does not require that the fetus be a stranger. It is hardly obvious that the conscript would
have a duty to stay hooked up to an acquaintance, a friend or relative, or perhaps even her
own child. While I happen to think a parent would have a pro tanto duty to stay plugged in
to keep her child alive, it doesn't matter for my account. Even if parents do not have a duty
to bear burdens on a par with those of pregnancy to keep their born child alive, they clearly
have a far stronger duty to prevent injury to their own child than to an acquaintance; just as
clearly, the limits of that duty are debatable and context-dependent (see Section VI).
9. McMahan, "Paradoxes," 634.

her reasons for aborting are unacceptable. Finally, I consider the claim
that even if an intending mother remains free to abort, doing so will not
preempt the wrong she commits by prenatal injury.
After addressing these challenges, I consider and reject an account that
treats the duties of an intending mother as unconditional. This account
imposes unreasonably demanding conditions for "willing" parenthood
and implicitly denies an intending parent the freedom to change her
mind. My discussion of these difficulties helps sets the stage for my own
account of those duties, which holds that a pregnant person's decision to
parent the child-to-be gives rise to more demanding but still conditional
duties of prenatal parental care.
On my account, prenatal care duties are conditional because they
become binding if and only if, having formed a firm intention to parent at
some point during gestation, the pregnant person chooses to carry the
fetus to term. 10 Those duties belong to a broader class of conditional
duties assumed by individuals who enter a preliminary relationship with
the intention of forming a more demanding one-a relationship they are
free to exit before the more demanding one is formed. If they do not exit,
those duties become unconditional, and the other party will be wronged
by their breach, even if the "breach" occurred when the individual was
still free to end the preliminary relationship. 11 Such conditional duties do
not rest on any responsibility the pregnant person may have for the exis-
tence of the fetus or its dependence on her. Rather, they rest entirely on
her deciding to parent the child-to-be and carrying the fetus to term. 12
They remain conditional so long as she remains free to terminate the
pregnancy.
After presenting my account, I point out significant affinities between
the duty of prenatal care and other "backward-looking" duties that do not
become unconditional unless followed by specific actions, omissions, or
events.
10. I will explain the reasons for this specific formulation at the end of Section VI.
11. Here and in what follows, I will refer to "breaches" that occur before a duty becomes
unconditional. This is shorthand for "breach-causing conduct occurring at a time when the
duty is still conditional." This conduct will constitute a breach only if the condition is
satisfied.
12. The argument I will make does not depend on the metaphysical claim that the fetus
and child are the same individual. If they are not, the child will still "inherit" the injury that
the pregnant person has a contingent duty not to cause or allow; even if they are the same
individual, that duty is not owed to the individual in his fetal "phase."

II. IS ABORTION THE MORAL BASELINE FOR PERMISSIBLE PRENATAL CARE?
Flanigan argues that if the pregnant person has the right to cause the
fetus's death by withdrawing life support, she has, a fortiori, the right to
cause it lesser harms. "If women are not required to remain pregnant and
provide gestational services to their unborn children, they are not required
to provide high-quality gestational services, either." 13 So long as the inju-
ries leave the child-to-be with a life better than nonexistence or abortion,
it is permissible for her to inflict them. Moreover, "since women who
commit prenatal injury still provide morally significant advantages on bal-
ance, [they are] still praiseworthy on balance." 14
Flanigan's claim seems plausible for some injuries caused by the preg-
nant rescuer. Returning to Thomson's analogy. 15 it is not difficult to come
up with variations in which only those who see morality as extremely
demanding would find it impermissible for the conscripted stranger to
seriously injure the ailing violinist to protect herself from lesser harm.
Imagine that her confinement would cause not only prolonged physical
discomfort but also the loss of significant opportunities and the atrophy of
valued skills. It would seem permissible for her to reduce that harm,
e.g., by unplugging for 8 h every day, even if that would harm the violinist
substantially more than it would benefit her. Further, it would be morally
better for her to do so than to withdraw. (The more demanding you take
morality to be, the higher you can rachet up the adverse impact on her.)
The claim that the pregnant person has only minimal duties of care as
a stranger to the fetus becomes even more plausible if we recognize
tighter moral constraints on a conscripted stranger than Flanigan acknowl-
edges. The stranger would surely face moral criticism for injuring the vio-
linist from malice, or by harmfully exploiting him for profit, even if the
violinist would be better off if she did so than if she unplugged herself.
13. Flanigan, "Prenatal Injury," 43.
14. Ibid. at 39.
15. Although she accepts Thomson's analogy, Flanigan does not draw on it in making her
argument. She shifts from an ailing violinist to an imperiled climber, kept from a fatal fall
only by a rope his climbing partner is holding ("Prenatal Injury," 35-38). She sees any effort
the partner makes to hold onto to the rope as supererogatory, so that while she has a moral
reason to hold on as long as she can (assuming some prospect of rescue), she would be
blameless if she let him go. But this is a more compelling case than Thomson's for claiming
minimal duties: the partner can't hold on forever! Because I think this example differs from
Thomson's in ways that strengthen the case for permissible withdrawal, I will stick with the
ailing violist in assessing Flanigan's claims.

These constraints do not arise from any moral difference between caus-
ing and allowing harm-an elusive distinction in a context where the con-
script's otherwise self-regarding actions, like swallowing a pill, may
directly harm the fetus. The more relevant distinction is between actions
and omissions that lighten the burden of support and those done for
opportunistic or malicious reasons.
Imagine that the conscript agrees to continue life support only if the
violinist performs a grueling concert schedule for the 9 months, turning all
the proceeds over to her. The conscript could expect to become wealthy,
while the violinist would suffer chronic joint inflammation and a perma-
nent decline in his overtaxed skills. I doubt that even Flanigan would
regard the conscript's action as deserving the faintest praise. 16 The preg-
nant person could be similarly criticized for, say, taking a bribe from a
rogue medical researcher to do experiments on the fetus with little scien-
tific value and a high risk of serious injury.
But even with these additional constraints, the core of Flanigan's a
fortiori argument remains: an individual who was free to decline to rescue
a stranger, whether a conscripted violinists or a fetus, owes that stranger
only minimal duties of care. The pregnant person may harm the fetus by
lighting her "burden of carriage" so long as she leaves the child-to-be with
a life better than abortion.
In treating abortion as a moral baseline for prenatal care, it is not nec-
essary to rely on the claim that choosing to gestate is supererogatory. As
Linda Eggert has recently argued, 17 the rescuer gets no credit for a sacri-
fice she has already made merely because it was supererogatory; she will
have the same duties to those she rescues as she would now face if the
prior act had been required or coerced. After all, like the conscripted vio-
linist, many pregnant people did not volunteer for a rescue mission.
Rather, finding themselves placed on such a mission by accident or coer-
cion, they are permitted to drop out. It is the continuing burdens of gesta-
tion that keep it supererogatory and justify suboptimal rescues.
16. Some would judge it impermissible for the conscript to harmfully exploit the violinist
this way rather than detach herself, although he would readily agree to her terms as the price
of survival. But even for those who would find it permissible, her course of action would
surely warrant moral criticism.
17. Linda Eggert, "Supererogatory Rescues," The Journal of Philosophy 120, no. 5 (2023):
229-56.

Because of those burdens, neither the conscript violinist nor the preg-
nant person faces a classic All-or-Nothing problem. 18 In such cases, a res-
cuer who has declined the permitted option of doing nothing is required
to do what is best rather than what is merely better-if she can do the best
at no additional cost. An agent is not required to enter a burning building
to save strangers, but if she does, she must save two rather than one if she
can do so at no greater cost. Clearly, continued gestation does have signifi-
cant additional costs, and adhering to a more-than-minimal standard of
care significantly adds to them. But will any further cost exempt the res-
cuer from a higher standard? 19
Eggert argues that the permissibility of a "suboptimal rescue" depends
on whether the further cost of an optimal rescue would exempt the res-
cuer from the ordinary duty of "easy rescue" 20 -in the above example,
whether saving the second person as well would count as an easy rescue.
While it is debatable when a sacrifice becomes too great for easy rescue,
continued gestation far exceeds any reasonable limit even under a mini-
mal standard of care. Yet, it may still seem that a pregnant person willing
to bear these formidable burdens would be wrong to abort or to cause
substantial fetal injury just to avoid a slight additional cost, for example,
foregoing a cosmetic treatment that may injure the fetus.
One way of accounting for the sense that the pregnant person would be
wrong to abort or risk serious fetal injury in such cases is to treat the bur-
dens she is willing to bear, along with those already borne, as the baseline
for determining if additional sacrifices would be too great for an easy res-
cue. In effect, the burden that the pregnant person is committed to bear-
ing could be seen as a sunk cost. If so, the further cost of foregoing a
cosmetic treatment would not exempt her from a duty of easy rescue.
It would, however, be unreasonable to assess that additional burden in
isolation. Someone willing to bear continuing burdens far exceeding the
cost of easy rescue is entitled to set a limit, one that may be exceeded by a

small additional cost. Assessing each incremental burden separately would
make the rescuer liable to endless sacrifice. Still, there may be a recalci-
trant feeling that it would be wrong for the intending mother to injure the
fetus, let alone abort it, solely to gain some small benefit. But if so, it
would be because she imposed significant harm for a trivial reason-a
possibility I take up in Section IV. Such cases, however, will be exceedingly
rare. If a minor loss is ever a deal breaker, it is likely because of its cumu-
lative impact on a very demanding rescue. Small pleasures confer large
benefits in this context, lightening burdens that might otherwise become
oppressive.
Eggert's account is also helpful in seeing why the conscripted stranger
and pregnant person are not permitted to take profitable advantage of the
helpless dependence of the violinist and fetus. In both cases, the rescuer
still faces ordinary duties against exploitation. Forgoing the opportunity to
exploit the victim should not be regarded as a "further cost" of rescue.
There is, however, another significant challenge to treating abortion as
the moral baseline for prenatal care. Thomson's rationale for abortion
rests on the fetus' threat to the pregnant person's right to bodily noninte-
rference. The only way to eliminate that imposition is to abort; burden-
lightening measures harm the fetus without ending its interference with
the pregnant person's body. 21 But while those measures do not end fetal
interference, they mitigate it. As a response to bodily imposition, they are
hardly a non-sequitur.
Other rights against bodily interference can be partially enforced as
well, permitting those facing a rights-violation to reduce their harm with-
out eliminating the violation. Rather than evict a trespasser, a property
owner can confine them to a small area for a short time. An individual fac-
ing a lethal attack she cannot escape is permitted to risk her own injury by
inflicting a nonfatal wound. 22 If rights to bodily autonomy, property, and
self-protection can be completely waived, they can be partially waived
as well.
Admittedly, unlike other cases of partial enforcement, most of the mea-
sures permitted by a lower standard of prenatal care do not directly miti-
gate the rights-infringement. But it is not clear why permissible mitigation

bodily integrity may be even clearer if the lethal threat she faces is not intentional.

should be limited to direct measures. First, measures that directly mitigate
fetal imposition would hardly seem more justifiable than typical burden-
lightening ones. A pregnant person about to compete in an athletic com-
petition would be no more justified in taking a pill to reduce the amount
of nutrients the fetus extracted from her body than in adopting a grueling
training regimen with the same moderately harmful impact on the fetus.
Second, indirect mitigation seems permissible as a response to other
rights-infringements as well. For example, the property owner may be held
to a lower standard of care for a trespasser than a guest and, of course,
the target of lethal aggression has little if any duty of care toward the
aggressor. The morally significant distinction is not between direct and
indirect mitigation of the burden, but, as I claimed above, between mea-
sures serving to directly or indirectly reduce the burden imposed, and
those serving to exploit the imposition.
In theory, the fetus could lack a right not to be aborted but have a right
not to be (unintentionally) poisoned with alcohol or injured by contact
sports. It would be difficult, however, to see the source of such a limited
right. After all, the reason the fetus lacks a right to continued gestation is
that the mother has a right to control her own body; to engage in conduct
that would count strictly as self-regarding in most other circumstances.
That right presumably extends to the beverages she drinks and the activi-
ties she pursues, but not to exploitation or malicious abuse.
As a stranger to the fetus, then, the pregnant person would still have
considerable latitude in subjecting it to risk or harm that left the child-
to-be with a life worth living. Her freedom to lighten the burdens of sup-
port would extend beyond protecting herself from harm. She could engage
in rewarding activities like contact sport that subjected the fetus to risk or
harm greater than the benefits they afforded her. We might be less
inclined to praise her than we would if she soldiered through pregnancy
with all the precautions now expected of pregnant people. But, given that
she still took on a significant burden to enable a stranger to have a life
worth living, she would not have wronged the child-to-be if she remained
a stranger to the fetus.
III. CAN A PREGNANT PERSON REMAIN A STRANGER TO A FETUS SHE INTENDS TO GESTATE?
It may be difficult to see how the pregnant person can remain a stranger
to the fetus if she foregoes abortion. Either she intends to parent the child

she will bear, or she is carrying the fetus as the agent of prospective par-
ents. In both cases, she is no longer a stranger to the fetus: in the former,
she may already regard it as her child; in the latter, she has agreed to
treat it (more or less) as if it was going to become her child. In both cases,
it may have been plausible to see her as a stranger to the fetus initially, at
least in an accidental or unwanted pregnancy. But she is now carrying it
as, or for, a parent.
Elizabeth Brake makes this assumption explicit, asserting that unless a
pregnant person plans an adoption, she becomes a parent simply by
choosing to carry the fetus to term: If abortion is an option, then choos-
ing to continue a pregnancy without making plans for adoption constitutes
accepting the role of a parent. 23 But why, on Brakes voluntarist account
of parental duties, should a pregnant person without adoption plans have
no options except abortion and parenthood? Given the formidable
demands of parenting, which Brake emphasizes, it seems unreasonable to
impose those duties on a pregnant person just because of her passivity.
Even if, as Brake claims, those duties are in large part conventional, it is
doubtful that under present conventions, voluntarily gestating to term
without having tried to arrange an adoption constitutes acceptance of a
parental role.
There are certainly cases in which a pregnant person would not accept
a parental role merely by continuing to gestate without pursuing adoption.
Consider a woman pregnant from a brutal gang rape. Even if she is unwill-
ing to abort, she may view the fetus not only as a stranger, but as a hostile
one, an extension of the violation she experienced. Her fear or shame may
make it difficult for her to pursue adoption plans, despite lacking the
slightest desire to parent the child.
But why should extenuating circumstances be needed to reject the pre-
sumption that a pregnant person has accepted a parental role? Why not
require affirmative consent for such a demanding role? The affirmation
need not be formal or explicit; Brake herself mentions buying baby clothes
and taking the child home, 24 and there are many other forms of tacit
acceptance.

24. Ibid.

One basis for treating passivity as consent to a parental role would be
that a pregnant person who carries the fetus to term is responsible for cre-
ating an extremely needy being, who can be expected to lead a short,
painful life unless those needs are met. But meeting them usually requires
someone to take on a parental role. So, a pregnant person who gestates
without taking on that role, or arranging for someone else to, risks con-
signing the child to a very grim existence.
That may have been true, and may still be true, in many places-but
perhaps fewer than might be supposed. In many poorer societies, child-
rearing by extended families may significantly mitigate the harm from a
pregnant persons rejection of a parental role. And in many wealthier soci-
eties, a newborn brought to a safe harbor-a designated hospital, for
example-has reasonable odds of a decent life.
If a pregnant person can carry a fetus to term without assuming the
role of a parent or proxy, she need not wrong the child by failing to exer-
cise the level of care such a role demands. It may be helpful to offer an
example, a case in which a pregnant person with no intention of parenting
remains a stranger to her fetus despite carrying it to term without adop-
tion plans, and in which ignorance, poverty, or unusual burdens do not
excuse a failure to adhere to a parental standard of care. In such a case, I
suggest, the pregnant person would have no greater duty to the fetus or
the child-to-be than to provide it with reasonable odds of a decent life.
Carriers Conundrum: A childless-by-choice woman experiences a
contraceptive failure. She had taken significant precautions not only
because she did not want to parent a child but also because she has reser-
vations about abortion. Despite her reservations, she feels no attachment
to the fetus she carries. But she is reluctant to pursue adoption for several
reasons: she dreads the highly personal interviews adoption agencies
require; she wants to retain the option to abort despite her reservations;
and she feels that arranging an adoption would be taking ownership of a
fetus for whom she lacks any maternal or proprietary feelings. Once the
child is born, she plans to drop it off at her local safe harbor facility,
which has excellent placement services. Meanwhile, she is getting ready
for a long-planned once-in-a-lifetime trip to view a melting Antarctic
glacier.
At an ob/gyn visit a few days before her planned departure, the ultra-
sound reveals that the fetus has a spinal curvature that will likely cause
frequent discomfort and reduced mobility, precluding most strenuous

athletic and recreational activities. While this condition can be mitigated
by intensive therapy, there is no postnatal cure. Fortunately, safe prenatal

The woman believes that the child would be significantly better off with
the surgery and that no responsible mother would decline it. But she
does not regard herself as a mother, or a prospective mother. She also

VII. PRENATAL PARENTAL CARE AS A DISTINCTIVE TYPE OF CONDITIONAL DUTY
VII.A. A Doubly Conditional Duty
The distinctive character of prenatal parental duties can be seen by com-
paring them to a broad class of conditional duties analyzed by Tina
Rulli. 64 Such duties arise when: (1) the agent chooses a morally better
option A over the morally worse but still permissible -A; (2) The choice of
A creates a choice between B and C and requires the agent to pick the
optimal B, although both options are better than -A. Rulli divides condi-
tional obligations into two types. In Type I cases, the agent has a pre-
existing duty to do B, but is exempted because of its cost-a cost she
assumes by choosing A. In Type II cases, there is no preexisting duty to do
B; the duty is created by the choice of A. 65 All-or-Nothing cases are reg-
arded as Type I by those who recognize a pro tanto duty of rescue: if the
agent chooses to bear the costs that rendered the duty optional, she must
then choose the optimal rescue when theres no further cost. Rulli
observes that many Type II obligations arise from the choice to enter into
a special relationship. The specific obligations arising from that choice
need not be voluntarily assumed, so long as the relationship itself is. 66
The prenatal care duties I have described do not fit neatly into either
category. They are not Type I obligations: because pregnancy imposes sig-
nificant additional costs until birth, an easy-rescue duty is never triggered
by the decision to continue gestation. The duties of the intending mother
are closer to Type II obligations in being created by entering a special rela-
tionship. But once created, they remain conditional. They do not become
binding unless a further condition is satisfied-the intending mother must
carry the fetus to term. 67

I have saved for last what is arguably the most relevant comparison,
between a backward-looking duty of fetal care and Elizabeth Harmans
view that the moral status of the early fetus depends on whether it ever
becomes conscious. 72 Harmans account shares a central feature with
mine: for both, present facts alone cannot determine whether the preg-

VIII. CONCLUSION
I have argued that the prenatal care duties of an intending mother cannot
rest solely on her decision to continue gestation or her present intention
to parent but do not become binding until she has carried the fetus to
term. They are duties of a distinctive kind, assumed by an agent for whom
they remain conditional during the time they must be fulfilled and
directed toward an being whose right to fulfillment depends on the agents
future actions.
